credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Starships jump from rest to large fractions of light speed in seconds with crew unharmed; 'inertial dampers' cancel acceleration
critique: Humans tolerate only ~3 g; at that limit it would take ~2.5 months to reach half light speed, and sudden acceleration would turn the crew into 'chunky salsa'; inertial dampers amount to suspending Newton's laws and are never explained
status_reason: Basic Newtonian mechanics and human g-tolerance; no known mechanism shields bodies from inertial forces (equivalence principle).

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Crews travel near light speed on long missions yet stay in sync with Starfleet Command and home time
critique: Special-relativistic time dilation means a 10-year crew mission near light speed could correspond to ~25,000 years at home; commanders back home would have retired; a quarter-light-speed cap keeps clocks synchronized but makes ships far too slow
status_reason: Time dilation is experimentally confirmed (muon lifetimes, GPS, atomic clocks on aircraft).

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Warp drive lets ships travel faster than light by warping space
critique: GR permits space to expand behind and contract ahead of a ship, but it needs exotic negative-energy matter never observed and a gravitational field whose creation would require more energy than the Sun emits over its whole lifetime
status_reason: The negative-energy requirement still holds (all warp metrics violate the energy conditions, Santiago-Schuster-Visser 2022), but energy estimates have dropped a lot since 1995 (Van Den Broeck 1999; White 2011; Bobrick & Martire 2021), so the 'Sun's lifetime output' figure is no longer the consensus number.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
work: Star Trek (franchise, incl. Deep Space Nine)
depiction: Stable traversable wormholes used as travel routes (e.g., the Bajoran wormhole)
critique: Holding a wormhole open would need large, long-lasting amounts of negative energy; negative energy has only been seen briefly and in tiny amounts (Casimir effect), so whether it is possible is unknown
status_reason: Still the standard view (Morris-Thorne; quantum inequalities limit negative energy); no macroscopic exotic matter has been found.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Holodeck creates solid, touchable objects and people from projected light
critique: Projecting light images is consistent with physics and limited mostly by computing, but 'there's no way to make an image of light solid'
status_reason: Photons don't form rigid bound structures at everyday intensities; lab 'molecules of light' (2013 Rydberg experiments) are microscopic and transient.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Transporter dematerializes a person and sends their actual atoms elsewhere
critique: Breaking the electromagnetic bonds of an adult-mass body would take over 1,000 times the world's annual energy output; moving the actual atoms as shown is not possible; at best you could send information and rebuild, vaporizing the original
status_reason: The energy scale argument (mc^2 and binding energies) is sound; quantum teleportation moves states, not matter.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Transporter scans every atom of a person precisely enough to rebuild them
critique: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle makes it impossible to resolve atoms and their energy states accurately enough to recreate a human pattern; resolving atom-sized detail at 40,000 km range would need X/gamma-ray optics with a 'lens' ~50,000 km across
status_reason: Reinforced by the no-cloning theorem; quantum teleportation (demonstrated since 1997) needs pre-shared entanglement and destroys the original state, unlike the show's scanner.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Phaser beams are visible as bright streaks crossing empty space
critique: A laser beam in a vacuum is invisible except where it hits dust or a target; it is visible 'only at the point of impact'
status_reason: Light is only seen when scattered into the eye; interplanetary space has almost nothing to scatter it.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Crew hears explosions and ship flybys outside the ship in space
critique: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum ('In space, no one can hear you scream'), yet the crew hears external explosions
status_reason: Sound needs a medium; interstellar gas is far too thin to carry audible sound.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: An episode gives an object's temperature as -293 degrees C
critique: Blooper: absolute zero is -273 C, so -293 C is impossible
status_reason: Absolute zero is the lower bound on the Kelvin/Celsius scale; lab 'negative absolute temperatures' (2013) are hotter than any positive temperature, not colder.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: The alien Mother Ship, about 1/4 the Moon's mass, parks in geostationary orbit while the attack goes ahead
critique: At ~22,500 miles (about 1/10 the lunar distance) its gravitational pull on Earth would be ~25 times the Moon's; the resulting tides would flood coastal cities and tidal stress would trigger earthquakes and eruptions before a shot was fired; it would also perturb Earth's motion and could brake Earth's rotation
status_reason: Inverse-square gravity; tidal forces scale as M/r^3, so the tidal effect would actually be ~250x lunar, which makes the point stronger.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: 15-mile-wide alien saucers hover silently a few thousand feet above cities
critique: A craft that size (~100 billion tons) hovering that low must push on the air below with ~450 psi (~30 atm), roughly 30 tons per square foot; buildings collapse at ~5 atm overpressure, so the saucers would flatten cities just by hovering, whatever their lift mechanism
status_reason: Momentum conservation: any hovering craft must transfer its weight to the air below; at altitude much less than its width, the pressure isn't spread out.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: Downed alien city-destroyers crash to Earth and humanity celebrates victory
critique: A single saucer falling from ~1 mile would release ~10,000 Hiroshima bombs' worth of energy, comparable to a dinosaur-killing impact; accelerating one to 3 mi/s in a minute would need ~5x10^19 W, ~300 times the solar power reaching Earth
status_reason: Simple mgh with his assumed mass gives ~1.6e18 J (~25,000 Hiroshimas), consistent with his order of magnitude.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: The quarter-Moon-mass Mother Ship decelerates into Earth orbit
critique: Slowing an object that massive into orbit within an hour would require engines radiating almost 10 times the Sun's entire luminosity, from only 22,500 miles away, toasting Earth
status_reason: Kinetic-energy bookkeeping (½mv^2 over a short time) gives power of order the solar luminosity; no new physics changes this.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: UFOs at a secret air base fly at great speed and make instant 90-degree turns; human test pilots fly them
critique: A craft at ~twice the speed of sound turning 90 degrees in 0.1 s feels ~700 g; neither the pilots nor the craft's structure could survive that, so real alien craft would not move that way
status_reason: a = Δv/Δt ≈ 700 m/s / 0.1 s ≈ 7,000 m/s² ≈ 700 g; Newton's second law still holds.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
depiction: Mann's planet has frozen clouds and ice structures that hold up large overhangs and the crew walk on them
critique: Thorne named this the film's most troubling physics error: ice is not strong enough to support the frozen-cloud structures shown, though he called it minor
status_reason: Ice's compressive and tensile strength (~1-10 MPa) can't support km-scale floating overhangs in Earth-like gravity.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
depiction: Miller's planet orbits extremely close to Gargantua, where 1 hour equals ~7 Earth years, and isn't torn apart
critique: He first thought this was impossible, then calculated it works only if Gargantua spins extremely fast (very close to maximal) and is very massive (>=100 million solar masses), allowing a stable close orbit with huge time dilation and tolerable tides
status_reason: Kerr geometry allows it in principle, but the spin needed (within ~1e-14 of maximal) is far above the ~0.998 'Thorne limit' that accretion and radiation should cap real black holes at.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
depiction: Huge mountain-height waves sweep Miller's planet about once an hour
critique: Explained speculatively: the tidally locked planet rocks back and forth in Gargantua's tidal field, driving giant tides; the waves look like non-breaking solitons, perhaps like tidal bores; the rocking period would also need to be about one hour
status_reason: A forced libration can drive tides in principle, but a planet in a stable tidally locked orbit should damp the rocking, and later analyses (e.g., arXiv:1503.08305) find no worked-out model for 1-km waves.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
depiction: Astronauts and a planet sit near Gargantua's accretion disk without being irradiated
critique: Gargantua's disk is 'anemic': cool, no longer fed by inflowing gas, so it lacks the X-rays and gamma rays a typical quasar-like disk would emit and that would kill the humans
status_reason: Low-luminosity disks exist (Sgr A* is very faint, as EHT 2022 confirmed), but a disk shining as brightly in visible light as shown would be fairly hot and still emit UV/X-rays.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
depiction: A wormhole near Saturn makes interstellar travel possible (Thorne also dropped warp drive and FTL from early drafts)
critique: The laws of physics forbid FTL travel and 'very probably forbid warp drives and traversable wormholes', though this isn't fully proven; the wormhole is placed in the film's speculative category
status_reason: Still the mainstream view: traversable wormholes need exotic matter; recent constructions (Maldacena-Milekhin 2018, the 2022 'wormhole-on-a-chip' simulation) are tiny, need special conditions, or aren't usable for travel.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; co-author with DNEG VFX team
depiction: Gargantua's accretion disk is shown symmetric in colour and brightness
critique: A real disk with material moving at ~0.55c would be Doppler-shifted and beamed: blue and very bright on the approaching side, red and dim on the receding side (frequency factors ~1.5 and ~0.4 with ~20% gravitational redshift); the filmmakers deliberately left this out to avoid confusing audiences
status_reason: Confirmed by Event Horizon Telescope images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022), which show strong brightness asymmetry from relativistic beaming.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; co-author with DNEG VFX team
depiction: Gargantua's on-screen image has a nearly circular shadow and centred disk
critique: The story's huge time losses need a near-maximally spinning hole (a/M≈1), whose shadow is flattened on one side with an off-centre disk; for visual clarity the filmmakers rendered it with spin a/M=0.6, inconsistent with the plot
status_reason: Standard Kerr ray-tracing result; EHT work confirms the spin-dependent shadow shapes such codes predict.

credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica, Eureka, Gravity
depiction: Galactica (over a km long) jumps into New Caprica's atmosphere, falls in a 'belly flop', launches Vipers and jumps out intact (episode 'Exodus, Part 2')
critique: A ship that size plunging into an atmosphere would 'do what Columbia did' and break up; he let the scene stand for its 'coolness factor'
status_reason: Aerodynamic and thermal loads on a huge non-aerodynamic hull are severe, but since the ship arrives by FTL jump with little orbital velocity, it wouldn't get Columbia-style reentry heating, so breakup isn't certain.

credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
depiction: Galactica rams the Cylon Colony at speed after jumping in about 100 m away (series finale 'Daybreak')
critique: With KE = ½mv², a ship that close couldn't build much speed even at 'flank speed' over ~100 m, so the ram couldn't deliver the energy implied
status_reason: Basic kinematics: v = √(2ad) is small for any survivable acceleration over 100 m.

credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
depiction: Ships have uniform artificial gravity from deck-plate generators; 'zero-g' is rarely shown
critique: FTL and artificial gravity have no known physics; a line of gravity generators would make a cylindrical field falling off as 1/r (not 1/r²), so hallway floors would effectively bow; spin gravity on a ring ship would need fast rotation and has its own problems; zero-g is mostly avoided for production reasons
status_reason: Gauss's-law geometry gives 1/r for line sources; no mechanism for artificial gravity other than acceleration/rotation is known.

credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
depiction: Humanoid Cylons are physically indistinguishable from humans, yet Baltar builds a 'Cylon detector'
critique: The Cylons' 'silica pathways' mean SiO2 (glass), which is inert, so a Cylon would show an anomalously high silica level in a mass spectrometer, which makes a detector plausible
status_reason: Mass spectrometry readily measures elemental silicon abundance; human tissue has very little silicon.

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
depiction: Astronauts at Hubble reach the ISS with jetpack and spacesuit oxygen
critique: From Hubble's orbit you can't reach the ISS on one spacewalk's oxygen; the trip is at least about LA-to-Mexico-border distance; he suggested a telescope in a closer orbit, but the production kept Hubble for drama
status_reason: Hubble (~540 km, 28.5°) and ISS (~420 km, 51.6°) are in different orbital planes; the plane change alone needs km/s of delta-v, far beyond an MMU.

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
depiction: A debris cascade from a destroyed satellite shreds spacecraft and keeps returning
critique: The premise rests on the Kessler Syndrome; the scale of damage is plausible 'for the level of scientific veracity needed to tell this story'
status_reason: Kessler cascades are a real risk (cf. the 2021 Russian ASAT test debris), but they develop over years, and debris from one breakup wouldn't hit objects in very different orbits within hours.

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
depiction: The shuttle is hit by debris and sent spinning rapidly with Dr. Stone attached to the arm
critique: Spin rate depends on impactor speed and mass; he isn't sure the film's spin is realistic, and the wing would more likely be sheared off than the orbiter sent spinning
status_reason: Hypervelocity (~km/s) impacts of small debris punch through or shear structures; they transfer little angular momentum to a 100-tonne orbiter.

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
depiction: Stone is spinning on the end of the shuttle's robotic arm and Kowalski tells her to detach so he can rescue her
critique: The arm is far more massive than the astronaut on it, so it's much more realistic to find enough delta-v to stop Stone alone; on release her velocity is the arm's centre-of-mass motion plus the rotational component, which could send her 'a pretty good kick' back toward Kowalski and Earth
status_reason: Momentum and rigid-body kinematics: a released body keeps its tangential velocity, and its small mass makes it easier to arrest than the arm-plus-shuttle.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS (Centre de Physique Théorique / Laboratoire d'Astrophysique de Marseille); made the first computed image of a black hole with an accretion disk (1979)
depiction: Gargantua is taken to spin within ~1e-10 (or less) of the maximal Kerr value to allow Miller's planet's orbit and the 1 hour = 7 years dilation
critique: Theoretically possible but 'by no ways realistic': prograde matter is hard to accrete while retrograde matter falls in easily and slows the spin, so real holes should top out near 0.998 J_max
status_reason: The Thorne (1974) spin limit of ~0.998 still holds; spin measurements by X-ray reflection and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA give high spins but none near 1 - 1e-10.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; pioneer of black-hole imaging (1979)
depiction: The planets around Gargantua are lit and warmed with no star nearby, and astronauts aren't harmed by the accretion disk
critique: A normal accretion disk is millions of degrees and would fry the astronauts as they leave the wormhole (and Cooper later when he falls in); Thorne's 'anemic' sun-temperature disk would be optically thin, so Luminet doubts it could give a planet Sun-like light and heat
status_reason: Radiatively inefficient, low-accretion flows (like Sgr A*'s, measured by EHT/GRAVITY) are very dim and couldn't warm a habitable planet.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; pioneer of black-hole imaging (1979)
depiction: Gargantua's accretion disk is shown uniformly bright, billed as the most realistic black-hole image ever made
critique: Basic effects are missing: a thin disk's emission peaks in the hot inner regions, and gravitational (Einstein) redshift plus Doppler shifts and beaming make the apparent brightness strongly non-uniform and asymmetric; his own 1979 simulation already included these
status_reason: Confirmed by EHT images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022), which show the predicted beaming asymmetry.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; researcher on tidal disruption of stars by black holes
depiction: Miller's planet orbits just outside Gargantua's horizon without being torn apart
critique: Bloggers claimed it should be shredded, but the Roche limit for a 1e8-solar-mass hole and a ~1 g/cm³ planet (~1e13 cm) is about the gravitational radius, so the planet feels large tides but survives; the film is 'marginally correct'
status_reason: Roche limit scales as (M/ρ)^(1/3) while horizon radius scales as M, so very massive holes have Roche limits near or inside the horizon, consistent with observed tidal disruption events around lower-mass SMBHs.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: Kilometre-high waves sweep Miller's planet about once an hour
critique: He suspects an inconsistency: a tidal 'wave' is really a fixed bulge the planet rotates through, but with tides this strong the planet should tidally lock almost instantly (he estimates ~1 ms), after which the water stays put pointing at the hole, so no periodic waves
status_reason: The tidal-locking argument is sound, but a ~1 ms locking time is implausibly short as an estimate, and Thorne's alternative (forced libration of a locked planet) isn't ruled out by it.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: The Endurance gets a boost from a slingshot past Gargantua while shedding part of the craft into the hole
critique: He reads this as a correct depiction of the Penrose process: a fragment dropped into the ergosphere on a retrograde orbit lets the rest escape with more energy, and repeated processes could extract up to 29% of a near-maximal hole's mass
status_reason: The Penrose physics is right (29% extractable for a=1), but the film and Thorne's book describe the boost as a slingshot plus Newton's-third-law ejection, not a true negative-energy-orbit Penrose process.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: Future humans in a five-dimensional 'bulk' build the wormhole and talk to our brane using gravity only
critique: Matches Randall-Sundrum brane cosmology, where matter and light are confined to our 4-D brane and only gravitational waves move in the bulk; creating mini black holes or wormholes (e.g., at the LHC) to exploit this is 'very unrealistic'
status_reason: The model matches RS theory, but LHC searches through Run 3 found no extra-dimension signals or micro black holes, and LIGO/Virgo GW170817 showed no gravitational-wave leakage into large extra dimensions.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: Murph writes the 'ultimate equation' uniting gravity and quantum mechanics on a blackboard
critique: The equation looks like the lowest-order effective action of M-theory in 5 dimensions; it's a nod to string theorists, but unification is unsolved and M-theory is 'probably not' the right framework; the idea that one equation solves humanity's problems is naive
status_reason: As of 2026 there is no experimentally confirmed theory of quantum gravity; string/M-theory has no direct empirical support.

credentials: PhD theoretical physics (Southampton); Professor of Physics, USC (later UC Santa Barbara); science advisor for Marvel films/TV and Star Trek: Discovery
depiction: Warp drive moves ships faster than light inside a spacetime 'bubble'
critique: You can write down the bubble solution (Alcubierre 1994), but like traversable wormholes it needs exotic matter/energy that violates the averaged null energy condition, which has never been seen, has no compelling reason to exist, and no known way to make or control it
status_reason: Reinforced by Santiago, Schuster & Visser (2022): all warp-drive spacetimes violate the null energy condition; 2021 'positive-energy' warp proposals (Lentz; Fell & Heisenberg) were shown to still need energy-condition violations or to be subluminal.

credentials: PhD theoretical physics (Southampton); Professor of Physics, USC; science advisor to Agent Carter season 2
depiction: Draft scripts called the show's exotic substance 'Element 0' because it 'did not fit anywhere in the periodic table'
critique: He urgently asked the writers to change it: the 0 slot is informally already taken by neutronium, neutron-star matter, which is physically nothing like the show's substance, so the name would confuse; it became 'Zero Matter'
status_reason: Atomic number counts protons; a zero-proton 'element' can only mean neutron matter (neutronium), as in neutron stars, which NICER/LIGO observations continue to constrain.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: The Endurance passes smoothly through a spherical wormhole near Saturn, shown as a tunnel ride
critique: Except for the correct spherical look on approach, most of Thorne's wormhole-crossing calculations were dropped as too confusing; a traversable wormhole is 'very improbable' and, if one existed, crossing it 'would not at all look like it is shown in the movie'; it's also unclear that normal-matter humans could safely cross the negative-energy region
status_reason: Ray-traced views (James et al. 2015, Am. J. Phys.) differ from the film's tunnel sequence, and no macroscopic traversable wormhole solution with ordinary matter is known.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: Cooper falls into Gargantua, survives, and reaches a tesseract from which he can affect the past
critique: In a Schwarzschild hole tidal forces at the centre would destroy him, but Gargantua's high spin gives an avoidable ring singularity, so idealized Kerr geometry lets him pass through as through a wormhole; black-hole physics gives 'no firm answers' on travel to the past
status_reason: The ideal Kerr interior allows this, but in realistic perturbed holes the inner (Cauchy) horizon is unstable (mass inflation, Poisson-Israel 1990; Dafermos-Luk 2017), so the passage through to other regions likely doesn't survive.

credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor of Interstellar
depiction: Inside the black hole Cooper uses a tesseract built by bulk beings to send messages back in time to Murph
critique: Time travel to the past is an open question: the film's rules were constrained less by known physics because 'we don't understand the laws of physics in that domain yet', so it sits in the speculative category
status_reason: Still true in 2026: no accepted theory of quantum gravity decides whether closed timelike curves are allowed (Hawking's chronology protection conjecture is unproven).

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: Crews often travel into the past and interact with history (e.g., visits to the 1960s and 1980s)
critique: Relativity doesn't strictly rule out time travel, but it creates paradoxes 'no sensible universe would allow'; replying to Hawking's 'where are the tourists from the future?' argument, he joked that they 'all went back to the '60s and nobody noticed'
status_reason: The paradox objection is widely held, but GR has closed-timelike-curve solutions and self-consistent (Novikov) or branching (Deutsch) models avoid paradoxes; the question remains open.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
depiction: An early episode ('Tomorrow Is Yesterday', 1967) has the Enterprise thrown back in time by the gravity of a 'black star'
critique: Krauss credits the show with depicting a black-hole-like object before the term 'black hole' was coined and widely discussed
status_reason: Collapsed stars were known (Oppenheimer-Snyder 1939) and Wheeler popularised 'black hole' in late 1967, so the show was early; but a black hole's gravity doesn't send ships back in time.

credentials: PhD physics (UC Berkeley 1972); Henry Semat Professor of Theoretical Physics, City College of New York; co-founder of string field theory
depiction: The transporter 'beams' Captain Kirk from ship to planet
critique: Real (quantum) teleportation doesn't move matter: it destroys the original and makes a twin at the destination ('you are destroying the original'); he puts a Kirk-style human transporter about two centuries away and notes beaming was invented to save the cost of landing effects
status_reason: Destroying the original is required by the no-cloning theorem, but a ~200-year timeline for teleporting ~1e28 atoms' quantum states is very optimistic; record quantum teleportation in 2026 is still limited to a few qubits.

credentials: PhD physics (UC Berkeley 1972); Henry Semat Professor of Theoretical Physics, City College of New York
depiction: Starships routinely jump to faster-than-light hyperspace/warp travel
critique: Physicists are inspired by warp drive and Einstein's equations allow warp-like solutions, but the energy ('gasoline') needed to power such a starship 'is far beyond anything ... in our laboratory'
status_reason: Warp metrics still need negative energy and huge energy budgets (Santiago-Schuster-Visser 2022), far beyond any lab.

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist (Cassini); science advisor to Virtuality and Battlestar Galactica
depiction: The starship Phaeton uses an Orion-style pulse drive fired by antimatter charges
critique: Based on Project Orion with antimatter charges instead of nuclear warheads; calculations suggest such a ship could reach about 0.5-0.8 c
status_reason: Antimatter has the right energy density in principle, but pusher-plate pulse drives are limited to a few % of c by plate ablation and heat, and the tonnes of antimatter needed are ~1e15x current production (CERN makes nanograms).

credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist (Cassini); science advisor to Virtuality
depiction: The crew make a 10-year round trip to Epsilon Eridani (~10.5 light-years away)
critique: The target was chosen because, at ~0.9 c and taking relativistic time dilation/length contraction into account, it is reachable within a ten-year round trip of crew time
status_reason: 21 ly at 0.9 c is ~23 Earth years but ~10 years of proper time (γ ≈ 2.3), ignoring acceleration phases; Epsilon Eridani's distance (10.5 ly) is confirmed by Gaia.

credentials: PhD high-energy physics (Manchester 1998); Professor of Particle Physics, University of Manchester; science advisor to Sunshine
depiction: The Sun is dying because a Q-ball (exotic supersymmetric particle) has lodged in it; a Moon-mass bomb was planned to reignite it
critique: In reality the Sun is not dense enough to stop a Q-ball, so the backstory is creative licence; he had the bomb scaled down from the mass of the Moon to the size of Manhattan, and said several inaccuracies were allowed to serve the plot
status_reason: Q-balls are still hypothetical (no detection at LHC or in dark-matter searches), and a weakly interacting relativistic particle would pass through solar plasma; any bomb is negligible next to the Sun's ~4e26 W output.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: The Millennium Falcon banks like an aircraft when it turns in space
critique: Planes bank because they turn using air pressure on their wings; in space wings play no part in propulsion, so there's no reason to bank. It's done because 'it looks good'
status_reason: Spacecraft change direction by thrust vectoring and attitude control; no aerodynamic lift exists in vacuum.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: Voyager (like the Enterprise) banks into turns and lifts its warp nacelles just before going to warp
critique: There's no air in space, so banking and the nacelle movement serve no physical purpose; the answer to 'why?' is simply 'It looks good'
status_reason: Without an atmosphere, attitude changes give no lift; nacelle geometry has no known physical role in any real warp metric.

credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
depiction: Rotating spacecraft and stations create artificial gravity by spin
critique: Praised as a correct depiction: spinning a large structure throws occupants against the outer wall, which is exactly how long flights will produce artificial gravity; by contrast, small, rapidly spinning TV flying saucers would pin their crew to the perimeter and gain nothing from saucer aerodynamics in vacuum
status_reason: Centripetal acceleration ω²r is the only practical artificial-gravity method known; studies favour large radii (>~100 m) to limit Coriolis effects, as 2001's large wheel station does.

credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
depiction: Nuclear missiles hit the Cylon Colony, knocking it out of position near a black hole while the fleet holds station amid rocks and gas (finale 'Daybreak')
critique: Nukes striking the hull would vaporize material and impart a change of velocity (Δv) to the Colony; drag from rocks and gas around it would force the ships to keep thrusting to hold attitude and orbit
status_reason: Ablation-driven momentum transfer is the basis of nuclear standoff deflection studies (LLNL 2010s-2020s) and was seen in NASA's DART impact (2022), where ejecta boosted momentum transfer ~3-4x.

credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
depiction: A wormhole appears near Saturn, placed there by unknown beings
critique: A natural black hole/wormhole mouth this close is extraordinarily improbable (stellar black holes are ~1e-5 per cubic light-year locally), and a black-hole-mass object at Saturn's distance would wreck the solar system's stability; hence the film's pure-SF choice of an artificially made wormhole
status_reason: Gaia astrometry has since found the nearest dormant black holes (Gaia BH1, 2022) at ~1,560 light-years, consistent with their rarity; a solar-mass-plus object at ~10 AU would strongly perturb planetary orbits.
